description: The annotated reading as data (docs/reading-annotated.md): a careful reader's thoughts through the story, one per line, and the background knowledge they use. Each thought's id carries its earliest paragraph; `maps` points to the case cards that hold it.

background.text: Two crimes at the same place and time share a cause and a culprit. Exceptions: one caused the other; two agents acted independently.
In a detective story the obvious suspect arrested in the first act is usually not the answer, and the unimaginative policeman is usually wrong.
A detail the narrator spells out without need tends to matter.
A famous racehorse is recognised on sight; a loose one on open country is soon seen.
Powders, drugs among them, come folded in paper.
A guard dog barks at strangers and at the unusual at night, not at people it knows.
Someone who discovers a theft and a drugged guard raises the alarm.
Powdered opium has a perceptible taste; a strongly spiced dish would hide it.
An exactly-right coincidence is not to be believed when an explanation by intention is available.
Men take a coat off to work, not to stand in the rain.
A frightened horse kicks out behind; a shod hoof can kill a man with one blow.
A *blaze* is a white mark down a horse's face; markings can be dyed out.
An owner or trainer can bet against his own horse through agents and then stop it winning.
A man arming himself against intruders takes a stick, a poker or a gun, not a precision blade that won't fold.
People don't carry other people's bills; they have enough of their own.
A man living under another name needs an address where that name's post can reach him.
A Bond Street milliner's costume of twenty-odd guineas is far beyond what a trainer's household spends on dress.
Period belief: travellers clear out when there is trouble, to avoid the police, and couldn't sell a famous horse.
A careful man practises a delicate, unfamiliar operation before doing it for real.
A loose horse makes for its own stable or the nearest other horses.
A violent denial of an accusation, followed by giving way, means the accusation struck home.
A "faker" is a dealer who disguises horses (dyes markings) to pass them off.
Odds that shorten sharply mean informed money is coming in.
A tendon in a horse's hind leg can be nicked under the skin to cause a lameness that leaves no trace.

reads: the singular disappearance of the favourite for the Wessex Cup, and the tragic murder of its trainer
thoughts.text: Two events: a horse gone and a trainer dead.

holmes.note: names it as part of a blunder

thoughts.text: Whoever took the horse killed the trainer. The reader holds this without noticing it; it has to be broken later (`t68.3`).

reads: points about the case which promise to make it an absolutely unique one
thoughts.text: Holmes calls the case unique, so the obvious explanation is likely to be wrong.

reads: You would oblige me by bringing with you your very excellent field-glass.
thoughts.text: An object asked for by name, so a reader might expect it to matter. It is used only to watch the race (¶199) and carries no inference. A player who instead files it as a prediction shouldn't be penalised, and nothing should follow from it.

reads: the telegraph posts upon this line are sixty yards apart, and the calculation is a simple one
thoughts.text: Holmes's speed calculation shows his method and carries no case content.

reads: the art of the reasoner should be used rather for the sifting of details than for the acquiring of fresh evidence
thoughts.text: The solution is in facts that are already public, so the recital that follows deserves a careful reading.

reads: to detach the framework of fact—of absolute undeniable fact—from the embellishments of theorists and reporters
thoughts.text: Some of what follows will be inference presented as fact; each item is to be sorted into seen or concluded. This licenses the WEIGH moves below.

reads: I could not believe it possible that the most remarkable horse in England could long remain concealed
beyond the arrest of young Fitzroy Simpson nothing had been done
thoughts.text: The horse has been missing since Tuesday morning in thinly populated country.
Where can a famous horse be hidden for days?
{dead, in a pit or mine; taken far away; hidden among horses, at a stable; loose on the moor}. `bk.famous_horse` strains "loose": he would have been seen. "At a stable" is the live candidate.

reads: his abductor was the murderer of John Straker
thoughts.text: Holmes names the one-culprit assumption as part of his blunder.

reads: he was the first favourite for the Wessex Cup
enormous sums of money have been laid upon him
there were many people who had the strongest interest in preventing Silver Blaze from being there at the fall of the flag
thoughts.text: Who gains if he doesn't run or win: {people who bet against him, bookmakers, rival stables}.
That aim doesn't need the horse taken: injuring, laming or hiding him until Tuesday would do. This becomes a question once we learn the horse was led out (`t57.3`).

reads: a retired jockey
five years as jockey and for seven as trainer
a married man
no children, keeps one maid-servant, and is comfortably off
a small villa about two hundred yards from the stables
thoughts.text: Straker. (⚠ low: "comfortably off" is the baseline `t84.7` breaks; a first-time reader files it as setting.)

reads: three lads
only four horses in all
One of these lads sat up each night in the stable, while the others slept in the loft
half a mile to the north there is a small cluster of villas
Tavistock itself lies two miles to the west
about two miles distant, is the larger training establishment of Mapleton ... managed by Silas Brown
a few roaming gypsies
thoughts.text: The map.

reads: has always shown himself to be a zealous and honest servant
All three bore excellent characters
thoughts.text: Reputation reported from the employer's side, not observation. It counts a little against suspecting these people, and no more.
Only two stables are in reach: King's Pyland and Mapleton. If the horse is hidden among horses nearby, it is at Mapleton.

reads: the stables were locked up at nine o'clock
Two of the lads walked up to the trainer's house, where they had supper in the kitchen, while the third, Ned Hunter, remained on guard
the maid, Edith Baxter, carried down to the stables his supper, which consisted of a dish of curried mutton
it was very dark
She took no liquid, as there was a water-tap in the stables, and it was the rule that the lad on duty should drink nothing else

thoughts.text: The narrator names the dish. Weak now; it becomes strong at `t37.6`.
The no-liquid rule is spelled out in detail: the story is ruling out drink as a vehicle.
If the lad is drugged, the drug was in the food.
Who handles the dish between the kitchen and the lad?

reads: a person of gentlemanly bearing, dressed in a grey suit of tweeds, with a cloth cap
carried a heavy stick with a knob to it
the extreme pallor of his face and ... the nervousness of his manner

thoughts.text: The description has no cravat. The maid later recognises one (`t35.5`) that she didn't describe here. That is small and leads nowhere certain, but it is the kind of gap a careful reader logs.

reads: I had almost made up my mind to sleep on the moor
I understand that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night
See that the boy has this to-night, and you shall have the prettiest frock that money can buy
a piece of white paper folded up

thoughts.text: A lost man wouldn't know the stable's night arrangements. The "lost" story is a cover: he came on purpose.
What is in the folded paper: {drug, money, message}. Most readers jump to the drug.
A poisoner would hardly ask a witness openly to pass the poison, and offer her a dress for it.

reads: the price of a new dress
thoughts.text: A dress returns at ¶84 and ¶91. The echo is an accident of the text and nothing follows from it.

reads: ran past him to the window through which she was accustomed to hand the meals
Hunter was seated at the small table inside
thoughts.text: Where was the dish during this scene: in her hands, on the sill, or on Hunter's table? The text doesn't say. The police theory depends on the answer.

reads: The girl has sworn that as he spoke she noticed the corner of the little paper packet protruding from his closed hand
thoughts.text: Sworn and specific: good evidence that he hadn't yet given the paper to anyone.

reads: You've two horses in for the Wessex Cup—Silver Blaze and Bayard
Let me have the straight tip and you won't be a loser
thoughts.text: His questions are those of a tout after information.

reads: Is it a fact that ... the stable have put their money on him?
thoughts.text: His question puts a pattern on the table: people inside the stable betting against their own favourite. ⚠ medium: a first-time reader takes the line as a tout's colour; using it needs `bk.lay_against`. The Bayard-specific version leads nowhere (Bayard is scratched, ¶192); the general pattern is the true motive.

reads: He sprang up and rushed across the stable to unloose the dog
Hunter rushed out with the hound
thoughts.text: The stable has a dog, set on intruders. A typical reader passes over it inside the action; the dog inference later rests on it.

reads: as she ran she looked back and saw that the stranger was leaning through the window
though he ran all round the buildings he failed to find any trace of him

thoughts.text: While Hunter crossed the stable to the dog, the stranger was leaning in through the window with nobody watching him. If the dish was on the table, he had a few seconds of opportunity.
If anyone came to the stable in the night, the dog should have made itself heard.

reads: The boy locked the door before he left it. The window ... was not large enough for a man to get through.
The importance of the point struck me so forcibly that I sent a special wire
thoughts.text: Access to the stable matters.
The stranger couldn't get in during the scene. Whoever later took the horse used a key or was let in.
Who has a key: {Hunter, the trainer, anyone with a copy}?

reads: he sent a message to the trainer
Straker was excited at hearing the account
It left him, however, vaguely uneasy
Mrs. Straker, waking at one in the morning, found that he was dressing
he intended to walk down to the stables to see that all was well
she could hear the rain pattering against the window
he pulled on his large mackintosh and left the house

thoughts.text: Chain of reporting: Straker's words → Mrs. Straker → police → papers → Holmes. What she saw (dressing at one, going out) is her own observation; the reason is Straker's statement, which she passes on in good faith.

reads: he does not seem to have quite realized its true significance
thoughts.text: That is a gloss, not an observation. It frames Straker as slow to worry, yet four hours later he is worried enough to go out in the rain.

reads: The door was open
Hunter was sunk in a state of absolute stupor, the favourite's stall was empty, and there were no signs of his trainer

thoughts.text: The door was opened with a key, from outside or from inside before Hunter went under.

reads: They had heard nothing during the night, for they are both sound sleepers

thoughts.text: Nobody mentions the dog. Someone came in the night and took out a horse, and the dog did nothing anyone heard. Most first-time readers miss this. It is the hardest move in the story, because nothing in the text points at the gap.

reads: for they are both sound sleepers
thoughts.text: This is the text's own defeater: the dog might have barked unheard. But the lads sleep in the loft over the harness-room, close enough that loud barking would be hard to sleep through. It weakens `t34.2` without defeating it.
Why was the dog quiet: {drugged too; barked unheard; the visitor was someone the dog knew}. Nothing says the dog was drugged (only the lad's supper was analysed, `t37.3`).

Straker went out at one, by his own account to the stables. Either he never got there, or he got there and raised no alarm: he didn't wake the lads in the loft about a drugged guard and an empty stall.

reads: They still had hopes that the trainer had for some reason taken out the horse for early exercise
thoughts.text: The household's first thought is that the trainer took the horse out himself. ⚠ medium: on a first reading this is just the household's hope.

reads: About a quarter of a mile from the stables John Straker's overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush
the dead body of the unfortunate trainer. His head had been shattered by a savage blow from some heavy weapon
thoughts.text: A blow, singular.

reads: he was wounded on the thigh, where there was a long, clean cut, inflicted evidently by some very sharp instrument
in his right hand he held a small knife, which was clotted with blood up to the handle
in his left he clasped a red and black silk cravat, which was recognised by the maid as having been worn on the preceding evening by the stranger
It was clear, however, that Straker had defended himself vigorously against his assailants
thoughts.text: An inference written as fact, including a plural ("assailants") that nothing observed supports. Re-file it as the police reading. This is the "embellishment" `t12.2` warned about.
Whose blood is on the knife: {an assailant's, Straker's own}? The thigh cut is "clean" from "a very sharp instrument", and he is holding one.
The coat is off. He set out in a mackintosh in heavy rain; a quarter mile on, the coat is on a bush. It stays weak until the wind is known (¶94–¶96).
{torn off in a fight and blown onto the bush; taken off}.
The cravat in his hand: {torn from the assailant (the police reading); planted on the body; Straker had it for some reason of his own}.

reads: Hunter ... was also quite positive as to the ownership of the cravat
He was equally certain that the same stranger had, while standing at the window, drugged his curried mutton

thoughts.text: Hunter couldn't have seen the drugging: had he seen it, he wouldn't have eaten the food. His certainty is a conclusion (the stranger was at the window, and later I was drugged) from a man just out of an opium stupor. Downgrade it to "Hunter believes".
The cravat identification is observation, and two witnesses agree. Keep it as fact: it is the stranger's.

reads: there were abundant proofs in the mud which lay at the bottom of the fatal hollow that he had been there at the time of the struggle
although a large reward has been offered, and all the gypsies of Dartmoor are on the alert, no news has come of him
the remains of his supper left by the stable-lad contain an appreciable quantity of powdered opium, while the people at the house partook of the same dish on the same night without any ill effect

thoughts.text: The opium went in after the lad's portion was separated from the household's: in the kitchen after dishing up, on the walk, or at the window.
The horse was led out of a locked stable to the hollow by someone with a key.
The curry now matters: it is the dish that hides the taste of opium. ⚠ low: the story dwells on the dish, but the step needs `bk.opium_taste`, which modern readers may lack.
The drugger knew or chose the menu. Exception: the drugger had a method that didn't depend on the dish.
The stranger came with his paper already made up and couldn't have known what was for supper. The drugger is of the household.
Who in the household: {Straker, Mrs. Straker, the maid}? The maid presumably cooks, and certainly carried the dish the whole way, so she had the most opportunity.
The maid drugged it, bribed by the stranger or on her own account. (Dropped at `t92.7`.)

Hunter corroborates the stranger's presence and manner, and she fled from him. And the drugging is only half the night: someone with a key took the horse out four hours later, and the maid leading a racehorse across the moor at one in the morning is a strained picture.
Missing for days despite a large reward and every gypsy on the alert.
The horse killed Straker: one crushing blow to the head, with the horse present at the time. ⚠ high: a first-time reader is primed for a human killer and rarely considers the horse before ¶212.

reads: Those are the main facts of the case, stripped of all surmise
thoughts.text: They aren't: the "assailants" and Hunter's certainty are both in the recital. The game could make this sorting an explicit task.

reads: Fitzroy Simpson. He was a man of excellent birth and education, who had squandered a fortune upon the turf
he inhabited one of those villas
bets to the amount of five thousand pounds had been registered by him against the favourite

thoughts.text: Simpson has a strong motive.

reads: Were he but gifted with imagination he might rise to great heights
the man upon whom suspicion naturally rested
thoughts.text: The unimaginative detective arrests the obvious man in the first act.

reads: On his arrival he promptly found and arrested the man upon whom suspicion naturally rested
thoughts.text: The police scenario in outline: Simpson drugged the lad, took the horse and killed the trainer. Holmes states it in full at ¶46 (`t46.1`).

reads: some information about the King's Pyland horses, and also about Desborough, the second favourite, which was in charge of Silas Brown at the Mapleton stables
When confronted with his cravat, he turned very pale, and was utterly unable to account for its presence
His wet clothing showed that he had been out in the storm
a Penang-lawyer weighted with lead, was just such a weapon as might, by repeated blows, have inflicted the terrible injuries

thoughts.text: Mapleton gains if Silver Blaze doesn't run.
The horse is at, or was taken to, Mapleton: it has a motive, the means to hide a horse among horses, and it is two miles away.
"By repeated blows" against "a savage blow": the police account of the weapon doesn't fit the wound as reported.
Wet clothing says he was out in the rain, which he admits for the evening. It says nothing about one a.m.
He goes pale and can't explain the cravat. That fits guilt, and it equally fits a man frightened to learn that something of his was found in a dead man's hand. Neutral.

reads: there was no wound upon his person

thoughts.text: Simpson has no wound, and there is no second assailant in the evidence, so the blood is probably Straker's.

reads: that the incised wound upon Straker may have been caused by his own knife in the convulsive struggles which follow any brain injury
It is more than possible; it is probable

thoughts.text: His own knife, his own thigh. Watson's mechanism (convulsions after the blow) is one option; the other is that he cut himself while using the knife. Keep the conclusion and leave the mechanism open.

reads: this Fitzroy Simpson, having drugged the lad, and having in some way obtained a duplicate key, opened the stable door and took out the horse
His bridle is missing
he was either met or overtaken by the trainer
beat out the trainer's brains with his heavy stick
either led the horse on to some secret hiding-place, or else it may have bolted
His bridle is missing
thoughts.text: The horse was bridled and led by someone who knew how.

The police theory leaves unexplained: 1. the curry: a stranger lucky in the menu (`t37.7`, `t37.8`); 2. the dog's silence while a stranger took the horse (`t34.2`, `t34.4`); 3. a duplicate key nobody has found (`t31.3`); 4. why take the horse out at all (`t18.3`); 5. how a stranger hides the most famous horse in England (`t14.3`, `t37.12`); 6. the trainer pursuing alone without waking the loft or loosing the dog (`t34.5`); 7. one blow against "repeated blows", and no wound on Simpson (`t40.5`, `t41.1`); 8. the coat off in the rain (`t35.8`).

Straker himself took the horse out. He went out at one, had a key, was known to the dog, belonged to the household that served the curry, raised no alarm, and took his coat off for some job. Against: his reputation, no motive in evidence, and he is the one who died. ⚠ high: every premise is on the page, but holding the victim as the instigator is a big jump for a first-time reader. The residue list (`t46.3`) is what pushes towards it.
If Straker, why? Only `t28.3` hints at a motive so far.
If Straker, what killed him: {Simpson met on the moor, someone else, the horse (`t37.13`)}?

reads: the evidence is purely circumstantial
We have quite come to the conclusion that he wounded himself in his fall
thoughts.text: The police accept the cut was self-inflicted. That removes the one piece of physical evidence that an assailant was hurt.

reads: He had a great interest in the disappearance of the favourite. He lies under suspicion of having poisoned the stable-boy, he was undoubtedly out in the storm, he was armed with a heavy stick, and his cravat was found in the dead man's hand
thoughts.text: Gregory's case, item by item: the motive is real; the poisoning is Hunter's conclusion; "out in the storm" doesn't fix the hour; the stick fits a weapon but not one blow; the cravat is real, but how it got there is open.

reads: Why should he take the horse out of the stable? ... Has a duplicate key been found ...? ... where could he, a stranger to the district, hide a horse ...? What is his own explanation as to the paper
thoughts.text: Holmes's objections are items 3, 4 and 5 of the reader's list, plus the paper. A reader who built the list can check it against his.

reads: If he wished to injure it why could he not do it there?
thoughts.text: Holmes puts injuring the horse on the table as a natural aim.

Turned round: what needed doing away from the stable? Something that couldn't be done within earshot of the loft, or that needed light that would be seen. It waits for the knife (`t81.2`) and the candle (`t78.3`).

reads: He says that it was a ten-pound note. One was found in his purse.
He has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer. The opium was probably brought from London. The key, having served its purpose, would be hurled away. The horse may be at the bottom of one of the pits

thoughts.text: The paper was money. The packet-equals-opium link, the strongest tie between Simpson and the drugging, goes.
Gregory meets each objection with a new assumption, not with evidence. A theory held up by patches is losing.

reads: He acknowledges that it is his, and declares that he had lost it.

thoughts.text: Unverifiable. If it is true, he most likely lost it on the moor that evening near the stables, running from the dog.
Someone passing the stables later picked it up, for instance a man going down at one in the morning. If it was Straker, why keep it: {to lay it on the stranger later, as a strap or tie}?

reads: a party of gypsies encamped on Monday night within a mile of the spot where the murder took place. On Tuesday they were gone.

thoughts.text: The gypsies have the horse. (Gregory's version adds Simpson leading the horse to them.)
Under the period belief their leaving is to be expected either way, so it points at nothing. It fits the police theory only by its timing.
They couldn't sell a horse everyone knows, taking him would bring the police down on them, and the theory explains nothing about the curry or the dog.

reads: I have also examined every stable and out-house in Tavistock, and for a radius of ten miles

thoughts.text: A search finds a horse only if the searchers recognise him, and his name says how they would: a blaze. A horse with the blaze dyed out is one more bay among bays. ⚠ medium: the reader needs `bk.blaze`, and the disguise isn't confirmed until ¶198.

reads: Silas Brown, the trainer, is known to have had large bets upon the event, and he was no friend to poor Straker. We have, however, examined the stables

thoughts.text: Brown adds motive. The search of his stables counts against `t40.4` only as far as `t64.3` lets it.
Silas Brown organised the night: the drugging and the abduction, through Simpson or someone else.

reads: And nothing to connect this man Simpson with the interests of the Mapleton stables?
Nothing at all.

thoughts.text: Nothing connects Simpson to Mapleton, and the curry and dog arguments point inside King's Pyland, not to Mapleton.
The one-culprit default breaks. The night is three stories: who took the horse out (inside), what killed Straker (open), who has the horse now (perhaps Mapleton). They may involve different people.

reads: There was a gleam in his eyes and a suppressed excitement in his manner which convinced me ... that his hand was upon a clue, though I could not imagine where he had found it
thoughts.text: Holmes has had the key insight in the carriage. Nothing new has reached him except Gregory's answers, so the clue is among facts the reader also has.
Go back over the recital with one question: which fact would make a man start? For a reader who missed `t37.6`, this is the prompt; a reader who already has it can confirm being there first.

reads: He has been in your service some years, Colonel Ross?
I have always found him an excellent servant.
thoughts.text: Right after his insight, Holmes asks the dead man's employer about the dead man's character. That is the question he would ask if the insight implicated Straker.

reads: a box of vestas, two inches of tallow candle, an A.D.P. briar-root pipe, a pouch of seal-skin ... a silver watch with a gold chain, five sovereigns in gold, an aluminium pencil-case, a few papers, and an ivory-handled knife with a very delicate, inflexible blade

thoughts.text: Five sovereigns and a gold-chained watch are still on the body. Not a robbery, and nobody searched him.
A candle as well as matches. Matches go with the pipe; a candle is for close work in the dark.
No lantern. He set out on a dark night to inspect the stables and took a candle stub, not a lantern.
If he lit a match in the hollow, a spent one may be in the mud there.

reads: It is what we call a cataract knife
A very delicate blade devised for very delicate work
it would not shut in his pocket

thoughts.text: A horse-trainer carrying a surgeon's eye-knife on a night when he expected trouble. This is the loudest clue in the story, and the story says so through Holmes.
Why carry it: {the nearest weapon; to operate on something that night}? The only possible patient within a quarter mile is the horse.

holmes.note: "no sane man would choose for a weapon"

thoughts.text: A man arming himself takes a stick or a poker.

He meant to injure the horse, delicately, away from the stable: away from the loft's hearing, by candle. The specific operation (nicking a tendon under the skin, ¶221) is specialist knowledge. The general form is enough to carry the chain, and the game should accept it.

reads: The tip was guarded by a disk of cork which we found beside his body
His wife tells us that the knife had lain upon the dressing-table, and that he had picked it up as he left the room
It was a poor weapon, but perhaps the best that he could lay his hands on

thoughts.text: Mrs. Straker's report is honest observation: he took the knife deliberately as he set out. Gregory's "best he could lay his hands on" is an inference, and a weak one: a man in his own house could lay his hands on much better.
The guard was by the body, so the blade was unsheathed in the hollow. That fits both readings.
Why does a trainer keep a cataract knife on his dressing-table at all?

reads: Three of them are receipted hay-dealers' accounts. One of them is a letter of instructions from Colonel Ross. This other is a milliner's account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen made out by Madame Lesurier, of Bond Street, to William Derbyshire
Mrs. Straker tells us that Derbyshire was a friend of her husband's and that occasionally his letters were addressed here

thoughts.text: A dead man carrying someone else's bill. Exception: settling it for a friend.
{Derbyshire is a friend, as Mrs. Straker says; Derbyshire is Straker, under another name}.

Mrs. Straker passes on what her husband told her: honest, but second-hand. "His letters were addressed here" is just how an alias gets its post, so her evidence for "friend" fits "alias" equally well.
Derbyshire = Straker, provisionally.
£37 15s at a Bond Street milliner, for a man "comfortably off" on a trainer's means. There is a lady with expensive tastes who is not, or not openly, his wife: a second household, and money pressure.
The motive: a man who needs money, and who controls the favourite, bets against him through others and makes sure he loses.

reads: Madam Derbyshire had somewhat expensive tastes
Twenty-two guineas is rather heavy for a single costume

thoughts.text: Holmes reads the bill line by line. The reader isn't shown the items, only that one is a costume of 22 guineas.

If Derbyshire is Straker, there are two versions: (a) Straker dresses his wife extravagantly under another name, and (b) there is another woman. Ask whether Mrs. Straker ever received that costume. "Friend" predicts no as well, so the test doesn't separate friend from alias; it separates (a) from (b).

reads: You wore a costume of dove-coloured silk with ostrich-feather trimming.
I never had such a dress, sir

thoughts.text: The dress Holmes describes must come from the bill: he is running `t85.3`. The reader has to supply this link. Fair-play note: the reader is shown the test and its result, not the item it tests.
Her denial is honest; she doesn't know what is being asked, which is why the trick works.
She never had it, so the costume went to another woman. (Holmes says as much at once, ¶93.)
Show Straker's photograph at Madame Lesurier's: the milliner will recognise him as Derbyshire.

The inside story of Monday night, every link either evidenced or a named default: 1. Straker, living a double life as Derbyshire with an expensive lady, needs money (`t84.6`–`t84.8`, `t92.4`). 2. He means to profit from his own favourite losing (`t84.8`). 3. He plans to lame the horse invisibly with the cataract knife, out on the moor, away from the loft 4. The household serves curried mutton; opium goes into the lad's portion, where the curry hides it (`t37.6`–`t37.8`). 5. At one he takes the knife and a candle, opens the door with his key; the dog knows him and keeps quiet 6. He picks up the cravat Simpson lost (`t60.3`; why he kept it stays open). 7. He leads the horse to the hollow, out of sight of the house, takes his coat off to work (`t35.8`), and strikes 8. One blow kills him; falling, he cuts his own thigh (`t35.2`, `t44.2`). The best candidate for the blow is the 9. The horse bolts. The nearest stable he could reach without being seen is Mapleton, where a searcher could
The maid as drugger: the inside story explains the drugging and the night visit with one person, while the maid version needs two, and she has no motive beyond a bribe she ran away from.
Who drugged the dish: Straker or his wife? The curry argument names the household; the dog and key arguments name the person who came at one. Holmes leaves the access question open (¶218).
a spent match in the hollow.
the coat was laid on the bush, which will show if the night was still.
the horse's tracks lead towards Mapleton.
the milliner recognises Straker's photograph.
the horse will be found in time to run, so Holmes will want him kept entered.
a careful man doesn't attempt a delicate operation cold, so Straker practised on something first. ⚠ high: reachable only by asking "would he do this cold?", and almost no first-time reader asks it.

reads: A short walk across the moor took us to the hollow in which the body had been found. At the brink of it was the furze-bush upon which the coat had been hung.

reads: These people always clear out when they hear of trouble ... They could not hope to sell such a horse.

thoughts.text: The ground near the hollow is hard and dry, so it took no tracks. Tracks survive only where the ground was wet.
Search the wet hollow on the line to Mapleton, with the horseshoe.

thoughts.text: Holmes on method. It repeats `t39.3` and carries no case content.

thoughts.text: The horse went from the hollow alone; he wasn't led away by whoever was with Straker. He bolted, and the man's tracks join him only near Mapleton.
Nobody left the hollow with the horse. That fits a death with no human killer present. It is consistent, not proof: a human killer could have fled on foot over the hard ground.
Who is the man?

reads: The double track turned sharp off and took the direction of King's Pyland

thoughts.text: The man set out to lead the horse home to King's Pyland, then changed his mind and turned back. He found the horse first and made his decision afterwards.

reads: Should I be too early to see your master, Mr. Silas Brown, if I were to call at five o'clock to-morrow morning?

thoughts.text: Holmes asks who is about at dawn. He is testing who could have found a loose horse early on Tuesday morning.
No groom would dare to hide a stolen favourite on his own account. Whoever did it at Mapleton had the authority to.
The man was Silas Brown: first up, master of the yard, with money on Desborough.

reads: As Sherlock Holmes replaced the half-crown which he had drawn from his pocket
thoughts.text: A tip offered and refused. (The game uses the half-crown as a starting item.)

an infernal lie!

thoughts.text: A violent denial, followed at once by an invitation into the parlour. Whatever Holmes said hit something true.

reads: His face was ashy pale ... he cringed along at my companion's side like a dog with its master
Your instructions will be done. It shall all be done

thoughts.text: Brown has the horse and has agreed to produce it ("it shall be there"), and the obvious place is the race.

reads: Should I change it first or not?
No, don't

Silver Blaze will run disguised, and Holmes intends a surprise.

reads: Of course you observed the peculiarly square toes in the impressions, and that his own boots exactly corresponded to them
thoughts.text: ⚠ fair play: disclosed late. Watson didn't report the square toes when they followed the tracks, so the reader couldn't have observed them.

reads: no subordinate would have dared to do such a thing

reads: from the white forehead which has given the favourite its name

reads: But his stables had been searched?
Oh, an old horse-faker like him has many a dodge.

thoughts.text: A "faker" is one who disguises horses: that is how the search missed him.

reads: he will guard it as the apple of his eye. He knows that his only hope of mercy is to produce it safe
thoughts.text: Brown now has every reason to keep the horse safe.

reads: the Colonel's manner has been just a trifle cavalier to me. I am inclined now to have a little amusement at his expense
thoughts.text: Character, not case: the explanation for the race-day surprise.

reads: this is all quite a minor point compared to the question of who killed John Straker

thoughts.text: Holmes leaves Dartmoor while calling the murder the main question. He wouldn't leave a murderer at large to be caught, so either he already knows and needs nothing more on the spot, or there is no murderer to arrest. Both point to the horse. ⚠ medium: a first-time reader takes this as Holmes being mysterious.

reads: I have every hope, however, that your horse will start upon Tuesday, and I beg that you will have your jockey in readiness. Might I ask for a photograph of Mr. John Straker?

reads: I have a question which I should like to put to the maid

thoughts.text: The question and its answer are never reported.

What did he ask: {who chose the curry that night; who was in the kitchen when the lad's dish was set aside; whether Straker came to the kitchen; about the dress}? Each fits a question left open (`t92.8`). The game could let the player write the question Holmes asked.

thoughts.text: For an expert who made `t92.14`, the prediction is scored. For everyone else it confirms `t81.5`: lameness is what the knife was for, and someone practised producing it.

reads: A long shot, Watson; a very long shot
this singular epidemic among the sheep
thoughts.text: For a reader who didn't predict it: Holmes expected lame sheep. Sheep don't go lame three at a time without a cause; Straker practised on them.

reads: To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.

reads: A child would know Silver Blaze, with his white forehead and his mottled off-foreleg
thoughts.text: Two markings, not one. A disguise has to cover both.

thoughts.text: A reader who made `t37.13` scores the hardest step in the story.
